body_markdown:
Cantonment is a Florida Panhandle town north of Pensacola, where something important happened in 1962. For Cantonment, anyway. It was the opening of the Southern Plywood Corporation, a state-of-the-art plywood factory housed in what was then called a “sprawling” series of buildings covering 135,000 square feet. Numerous residents would no longer have to take Highway 29 down to Pensacola or up to Molina to find a job. But four years later, the factory was sold, and it changed hands again and again until it ceased to exist.


> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/DXrwN_HDlde/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
>
>
> [A post shared by @floridamemory](https://www.instagram.com/p/DXrwN_HDlde/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)


There were not many businesses that needed 135,000 square feet, especially in rural Cantonment, and according to Pensacola native Stuart Wilson, several enterprises rattled around in the factory at 15 East Quintette Road until a military aircraft contractor finally moved in. The rail spur that runs right into the building dropped off large military aircraft, the factory overhauled them, and the refurbished planes took the rail spur right back out of town.


Then that went bust. And the factory that was once called “the gleaming new Southern Plywood plant” became Cantonment’s unwanted 20-acre eyesore.


Wilson was aware of the old factory—really, you couldn’t miss it—and when he drove up to look at what was left, it was a horror show. “It had sat vacant for four or five years, all the power lines had been stripped out of it, the roof was missing, the offices were gutted, it had been vandalized to the hilt.”


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


He bought it anyway, in September of 2020, and friends whispered among each other, wondering if Stuart was OK. He promptly had it stripped down even more, then he began to put it back together as the future home of[Velocity Restorations](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/now-from-velocity-restorations-dentside-ford-restomods/) . His crew loaded up everything they had at their old 18,000-square-foot factory in downtown Pensacola, “and we moved in here in July of 2021. Seven days later, we were up and running, building our first-generation Bronco.”


Indeed, Wilson was fast becoming royalty in the Bronco restoration world. Inspired, he’d sketched out plans for a rudimentary vehicle assembly line, and they built one. It worked. Then he added another, and another, and another—now four lines in all that produce a lot more than Broncos. A breathtakingly quick five years after that move-in, it turns out that 135,000 square feet isn’t enough. Wilson needs another 30,000 to house Velocity’s latest business acquisition, the star-crossed Classic Recreations, the Texas-based Ford Mustang restorer that Wilson bought out of bankruptcy. More about that in a moment.


Suffice it to say that Velocity Restorations, a business he and a friend started on a shoestring, earned Wilson some solid local-boy-makes-good credentials.


The actual executive offices of[Velocity Restorations](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/velocity-restorations/) are in a rectangular building, oddly constructed on concrete piers above a small man-made pond by a previous tenant. The Velocity staff seems to like it. You can fish off the railing on your lunch break.


Steven Cole Smith


Certainly, the abandoned Southern Plywood plant needed some sort of renaissance, and Wilson understands what that means. He joined the Navy at age 20, where he was trained in nuclear propulsion. That gave him the choice of serving on nuclear-powered ships or submarines; he chose the subs.


Wilson would head out on underwater deployments that lasted as long as 110 days—“I really enjoyed it,” he recalled, realizing how odd that might sound—and when he was back on land and had a break, he began buying real estate and flipping houses, mostly in Georgia. That was before he went *full* send and started building houses on spec. At the end of 10 years, he realized his real estate side hustle paid a lot better than the Navy, and with those long deployments, he was missing out on time with his wife and young daughter. He put in his retirement papers.


Then it happened. “In the span of six months, I got out of the Navy, the housing market crashed, I got a divorce and had absolutely nothing to my name,” Wilson said.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


He moved back to his hometown, Pensacola. He was 30. No furniture, not even a car. “All I had was a 1976 Ford Bronco that I had started restoring. It was in pieces in shops all around South Georgia. I collected the pieces and brought them back here.” His intent was to finish the Bronco and try to sell it. “My mom actually gave me a loan against her credit card to go buy a $4000 truck,” he said, and he took advantage of what was left on the credit card’s limit to pay for bits and pieces needed to complete his Bronco build.


He got a job as a plant manager, finishing the Bronco by working on it nights and weekends. “I sold it on eBay for $21,000. At the time that was a lot of money, but today—wow, we pay that for donor vehicles. I used that money to buy another Bronco, restored it, and made enough to hire a guy. And 14, 15 years later, here we are.”


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Wilson originally launched Velocity with a partner, fellow Bronco fan, restorer, and area native Brandon Segers. In March of 2022, Segers left the company. That put the reins of Velocity solely in Wilson’s hands. He has a trusted support staff, though, led by Cody Dabney, who came on board after meeting Wilson through mutual friends. Dabney was working at a nationally regarded restoration shop in Pensacola, where he specialized in paint and body work. He took on the same responsibilities at his new employer.


Cody Dabney


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Now, 11 years later, Dabney is Velocity’s director of products and operations, and consequently he had a voice in the company’s beyond-Bronco decision to expand to different models. The current count is 11, with more on the way.


Are these cars, trucks, and SUVs what you’d choose if you were Stuart Wilson? No question the Bronco essentially writes the checks at Velocity, but the plan is that growth will come through new products.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Certainly, research plays a substantial part in what will or won’t join the Velocity family, with the first question Wilson and crew needed to answer being: Are there enough of these vehicles still out there that we can acquire and restore? Every vehicle that Velocity and its restomod competitors send to market has to already exist, with the most critical part being its metal vehicle information number plate. Velocity has seven agents across America searching out, say, restorable[first-generation Broncos](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/your-handy-1966-77-ford-bronco-buyers-guide/) , and whatever vehicles will follow.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Similarly, a Velocity product might consist of using a brand-new front bumper, a brand-new rear bumper, and a whole lot of fresh parts in between, except for that VIN plate. That makes it a restoration, not an OEM-level new model, so it doesn’t have to meet the same federal standards that an OEM does. Is that a loophole? You tell us. But imagine what a Velocity-built Bronco would cost if Wilson had to engineer in, and then crash test, a dozen airbags. Absent this circumstance, there would be no 1966 Bronco that looks just like it did 60 years ago but starts every morning, stops hard every time you hit the brakes, has ice-cold air conditioning, and doesn’t drip oil on the driveway.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Velocity’s current model lineup begins with that inevitable Bronco, continues with the 1967-1979 Ford F-Series pickup—the F-100, F-150, and F-350; the F-Series was the first non-Bronco model that Velocity tackled, back in September of 2022. That enormous 1978 F-350, which is just now rolling out, is a Crew Cab, with four doors and a roomy back seat. It’s in response to requests from customers who wanted a heavy-duty truck with room for the whole family that can tow and do other heavy-duty truck things. It certainly has the power: The engine is[Ford’s 7.3-liter Godzilla V-8](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/ford-performance-super-duty-gozilla-v8-crate-engine/) , with a cast-iron block and aluminum heads.


Velocity


The price is downright heavy-duty as well: $459,900 to start, which gets you a build slot and a warning: “Due to the nature and rarity of the donor Crew Cab vehicle, the price shown does not include the purchase of the donor vehicle.” In other words, finding a suitable VIN-bearing, 1973 to 1979 F-350 Crew Cab with four-wheel-drive will likely send the sticker of this pickup to a half-million dollars, the priciest Velocity product there is. Well, for now.


Velocity


Like the Velocity Broncos, the smaller F-Series pickups are powered by the same 5.0-liter, 460-horsepower Coyote V-8, coupled to the Ford 10-speed automatic transmission.


Velocity


Velocity


The very methodical, 14-week build includes chassis fine-tuning on a dyno and a 500-mile test drive, with a trained Velocity employee squinting hard and listening attentively, trying to find issues to fix.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


There is also Velocity’s take on the 1967 and ’68 Mustang, either the beloved *Bullitt-* style fastback or a convertible. One example, due to be completed next month, is a fastback with the ubiquitous 5.0-liter Coyote V-8, boosted by a Whipple supercharger (figure around 800 horsepower) attached to Ford’s 10-speed automatic, and riding on a Roadster Shop chassis. (The Roadster Shop is a busy chassis builder near Chicago; its products underpin a great many hot rod and restomod projects, and Velocity is its biggest customer.) This top-level Street Series model starts at $384,900, and will be available in October 2026. Thankfully, some of the Velocity Mustangs are fitted with the very appropriate T-56 six-speed manual transmission— *so* much more fun than the automatic.


And the final Ford is, for our money, a gamble for Velocity; it will soon offer a run of new-old 1987-1989[Fox-body Mustangs](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/the-market-for-fox-body-mustangs-is-maturing/) . The company will initially build five, testing the waters to see if there are customers for a $279,900-and-up, 40-year-old model when there’s no shortage of nice, restored or at least cared-for notchback Mustangs LXs with the then-original 5.0-liter V-8 at a fraction of the Velocity price.


Cody Dabney believes a Fox-body Mustang will indeed sell, from what he’s hearing. “Usually our customers are connected to what they buy, some way, somehow, throughout their life. Maybe the family had one, their grandfather had one, they rode in it as a child, or they just thought it was cool, and they always wanted one. And now they’re successful, and able to buy one.” This Mustang certainly qualifies as a reward-yourself purchase, likely by people who were among the millions exposed to this 5.0-liter Mustang then; hundreds must be earning enough money by now to buy one, and that’s all Velocity needs.


Dabney doesn’t deny that Velocity’s willingness to tool up for this Mustang is a gamble: “Building a $400,000 Fox-body, you have to make sure it is going to appeal to the masses. It’s an expensive car,” he noted, but a potentially important one. The company philosophy, Dabney said, is “‘Let’s get into this ‘80s and ‘90s era, test the waters, and see if our customer base likes it.’”


Velocity


Velocity


Velocity


The Fox-body, tepid as it was by today’s standards, helped keep the performance-car flame lit during a grim period in American muscle, when 225 horsepower seemed like a lot. Velocity’s take adds about 485 additional horses, six more gears in the automatic transmission, a carbon-fiber driveshaft, three-piece, 18-inch billet wheels, a rigid Roadster Shop chassis, Vintage Air climate control, Recaro seats, and a BASF Glasurit paint job. Is it special enough to sell for Ferrari Amalfi money? We’ll see.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Velocity offers several models that carry a Chevrolet badge, including the[1967-1972 C/K pickup,](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/velocity-restorations-takes-on-the-chevy-c10/) a style that has truly been embraced in the past decade or so. Some of the Velocity builds have been significantly lowered, enhancing a slightly sinister personality that makes the C10 appear ready to leap from its haunches. Other builds retain a closer-to-stock appearance, the most appealing of which copy the era’s two-tone paint, consisting of white and almost any other color, including Hugger Orange.


In fact, there’s a handsome 1971 K10 painted those colors (C is rear-wheel drive, K is four-wheel drive) powered by the popular 455-horse Gen 5, 6.2-liter LT1 V-8 attached to a 10L80 10-speed automatic transmission, leading to a[Ford 9-inch rear](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/in-praise-of-the-ford-nine-inch/) , atop a Roadster Shop chassis.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Velocity’s Chevy pickups aren’t cheap—the orange and white one featured here costs $349,900, which is Ferrari 296 GTB money.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Then there’s the steady-selling[1969-1972 K5 Blazer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/we-drive-the-first-velocity-k5/) , of which Velocity has three, ready to roll, plus two more that will be finished in March. The cheapest of the five is a 1971 for $359,900, the most expensive is a ‘70 for $410,400. Specs are similar to the C/K pickups, with the LT1 engine and 10-speed automatic transmission.


Finally, we’ve come to the last vehicle in Velocity’s current lineup: The 1971-1980[International Harvester Scout II](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/velocity-modernizes-the-international-harvester-scout-ii/) . The Scout uses a Roadster Shop chassis and the GM LT1 and the 10L90 10-speed auto combination; the 10L90 transmission is beefier than the 10L80 used in the Chevrolet builds. The new chassis allows Velocity to swap out the Scout II’s leaf springs for adjustable coilovers, a big and tunable improvement. There’s a four-link rear and anti-sway bars on both axles.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Velocity has no Scouts in inventory, though there’s one listing for a 1975 Scout II’s coming-soon build, which is far enough out that a customer can still specify color, trim and interior. The listed price is a heady $407,900. “For the Scout, there’s almost a cult following,” Dabney said. “We’ve opened some eyes as to what is possible for the Scout.”


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


Unfortunately, it was raining when I visited Velocity, so my test drives of a half-dozen products were brief. Still, it was a linear experience—both the Ford and General Motors V-8s serve up plenty of power, and the two available 10-speed automatic transmissions meant, in theory at least, that you’re always in a gear that maximizes the available power. It’s hard to fault any of the interiors, especially the leather-appointed ones. And Velocity does a superior, mind-meld job of integrating modern features, such as the sound systems, air conditioning, gauges, and power windows, into the look and feel of the respective originals.


Of the vehicles I drove, the Bronco was the most buttoned-down, understandable since it’s Velocity’s signature product. The suspension is firm, but the ride isn’t punishing, and the Coyote V-8 makes all the right noises. As a daily driver, and Wilson insists those customers exist, it would work quite well. Similarly, the Scout II was a favorite, and it makes you wonder that if International had managed to hang on and develop the Scout over the years the way Jeep has the Wrangler, what an interesting vehicle it might be.


Obviously, Stuart Wilson and crew are clearly making good use of the plant’s 135,000 square feet, as well as the entire 20 acres it sits on. Those donor vehicles—remember, one is required per Velocity build—stretch along one side of the plant, and around to the rear.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


When Wilson decided to hold fast in his Florida Panhandle rather than move somewhere more visible, possibly with a larger workforce available—Dallas and Nashville were mentioned—he knew filling up his factory might be a challenge. Velocity has about 180 employees, with 300 the eventual target for Velocity, and maybe about 50 for Classic Recreations, the vintage Mustang builder that Wilson bought out of bankruptcy, and the reason he needs another 30,000 square feet.


That his projections say it’ll take 350 people to build his vehicles does not come as a jolt to Wilson; it’s something he envisioned years ago with the development of the assembly line system. He needs an employee who can work effectively at one station on the line, copying the OEMs. Ford doesn’t need a worker who can build a Mustang; they need a worker who can attach bumpers. And another worker to add the exhaust. Or bolt in the seats, or bolt on a fender.


“I was crazy enough to invest $20 million in the process,” Wilson said. For each build, there’s a 1200-page instruction book. One worker might be responsible for 40 pages, another for 50. “I can take a 22-year-old kid and have him building a Bronco in 12 weeks, doing stuff he’s never done before,” Wilson said. Every assembly line has nine stations; every vehicle moves from start to finish in 14 weeks. “I can also take a senior Ford mechanic who is tired of dealing with Ford, and the warranties, and the callbacks and other stuff, and he can come right in here and in eight to 10 weeks, he’ll be qualified to build a Bronco.”


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


That process, Wilson said, “opens up about 80 percent of your workforce.”


For the other 20 percent? Yeah, that’s a challenge. No manual is going to instruct an employee, from start to finish, how to paint a $400,000 Chevy Blazer. Dabney knows: That was his world. Now, his world includes helping find that 20 percent who deliver talent as well as skill.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


“The entire industry is struggling to hire people,” Dabney said. “It’s a dying art to build restomods. Younger people spend so much time on their phones or their computers, and they’re just not used to working with their hands. Sure, working here, building quarter-of-a-million-dollar vehicles is super cool,” if you’re a car geek, Dabney said. “But yeah, hiring is a challenge.” Walk in off the street and get hired, he said, and pay is $20 an hour. Pretty quickly, especially if you cross-train, “it can go up to $30 an hour, plus.” Wilson said that Velocity has found some qualified workers at trade schools like Universal Technical Institute, which has 17 locations across the country, and WyoTech, which operates a big campus in Laramie, Wyoming.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


And Velocity needs talented, skilled workers more than ever. A year ago, Velocity acquired what was left of Classic Recreations, the company that built retromod Ford Mustangs to order. It filed for bankruptcy in July of 2025, about 20 years after the company was founded in Yukon, Oklahoma, by Jason Engel. Classic had been licensed by Shelby American to build Mustangs that carried the Shelby name. Shortly before the bankruptcy was filed, Shelby American terminated the agreement. Classic marketed some special-edition Shelbys such as the Shelby GT500CR Centennial Edition announced in early 2024, of which just 10 units were planned, each priced at $625,000.


But word began circulating long before the bankruptcy that Classic could not fulfill all its orders. Wilson went to Classic to talk to the owners, then hosted them in Cantonment. The final discussion was in Velocity’s boardroom. They were not able to reach a deal. “And that was it,” Wilson said. “Until I bought it out of bankruptcy three and a half years later, almost to the day.” Wilson made a separate deal with Shelby, to continue the build of Shelby-branded vehicles.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


That Classic had filed for Chapter 11 was a bitter pill for its customers to swallow. Some of them had sent check after check to the company in hopes of getting the car they had ordered months before. That investment was essentially stricken from the books by the bankruptcy. Even if Classic had started a custom build, that uncompleted car would become the property not of its customer, but the new owner of the bankrupt company.


We were unable to reach the former owners—three brothers, who had moved Classic from Oklahoma to Flower Mound, Texas—or past executives of the company for comment. The bankruptcy and Velocity’s subsequent purchase of Classic is public record, and part of the deal required Velocity to decline when asked to identify or discuss the former owners. Kathryn French, Velocity’s brand manager, said this in an email: “Discussing the past does not serve us or our customers in any way—especially since it’s been over a year since we took ownership. We are focusing only on how we are transforming and elevating Classic Recreations now and going forward.”


Surprisingly, perhaps, Wilson decided to keep the Classic Recreations name, with a logo that has a tiny “Powered by Velocity” at the bottom. Wilson reached out to each affected customer with a two-part plan: *Let us finish your car, and we will give you ownership of the Mustang that Classic had been building on your behalf. But the kicker is that we will have to be paid for the work we do to finish your car.*


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


“When we took over Classic Recreations,” Dabney said, “it was a company that was failing, it was in peril, and there were a lot of customers who were going to be done wrong—they were going to lose their car, lose their build—we looked at it as an opportunity to help save part of the industry.” Wilson figures there were about 40 builds promised but never delivered. So far he has signed 22 of those customers to continuation contracts.


That said, Wilson points out that you can’t build these Mustangs, especially the Shelby cars, on the assembly lines he created. They must be constructed by that other 20 percent of his workforce, the diehard, old-school craftspeople. And that means what the new Classic Recreations will build is quite expensive.


The pre-bankruptcy Classic typically claimed in print that one of its Shelby Mustangs required four months and 2500 manhours to build, an investment Wilson is prepared to make. The upcoming builds for the 1967-68 GT 500CR Carbon, which will have a body made from carbon fiber, will start at $549,900 for the (cough) entry-level, 500-horsepower Stage 1. Stage 2, with 700 horsepower, is $624,900. And a Stage 3 car, with 900 horsepower, is $724,900, and adds carbon-fiber wheels, a carbon driveshaft, and carbon-ceramic disc brakes.


All from inside a 64-year-old ex-plywood factory, and a company founded by a man who had $21,000 in the bank and a credit card with a $10,000 limit.


Velocity/Nathan Van Etten


So expect Stuart Wilson, now 46, to end up with a 165,000-square-foot factory by this time next year, which is 164,750 square feet larger than the space where he built his first Bronco. Eventually, “I want to build around 300 to 400 units a year for Velocity, 60 to 70 units for Classic Recreations, across 10 to 12 models. Velocity will be around 300 employees then; Classic Recreations, probably 40 to 50 employees.” He pauses. “It sounds crazy, right?” He also expects to open Velocity’s first retail outlet soon, possibly near Dallas and/or in South Florida.


And he remarried—”My wife helped me finish that first Bronco in the garage”—and the little girl, who partly caused him to quit the Navy so he could spend more time with her, is 17 now. She’s joined by twin 10-year-old sisters.


To hear Wilson tell the tale, he makes it sound like the way the Velocity turned out is the way he envisioned it all along.


But it’s Cody Dabney, his right-hand man, who may have summed it up best: “I still feel like today, we’re just getting started.”


The post[Velocity Restorations: Big Dreams, Bigger Risks, Huge Rewards](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/velocity-restorations-big-dreams-bigger-risks-huge-rewards/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
